title: Reading a Thermometer
description: Recognize temperature scales and the visible parts of traditional liquid-in-glass thermometers.
cardDescription: Recognize temperature scales and the visible parts of traditional liquid-in-glass thermometers.
focus: Different instruments use different sensing methods. These clues specify the liquid-in-glass design where needed and distinguish a scale name from the liquid or glass component.
solvingTip: Check whether a word names a unit step, a measurement system, or a physical part. The shorter parts help cross the longer scale names.
words: Unit step on a Celsius or Fahrenheit temperature scale
Temperature scale with water freezing near zero at ordinary pressure
Temperature scale commonly used for American weather reports
Silvery liquid metal historically used in some glass thermometers
Type of colored liquid used in some glass thermometers
Reservoir at the bottom of many liquid-in-glass thermometers
Narrow glass passage containing the rising liquid column
Transparent material enclosing a traditional thermometer column
To determine the indicated temperature from its markings
Having a relatively high temperature compared with cool
Having a relatively low temperature compared with warm
Number at water's ordinary freezing point on the Celsius scale
Short printed line identifying a value on the scale

answerNotes.DEGREE: A degree is a step on these named scales. Their steps are not the same size, so the scale name matters.
answerNotes.CELSIUS: The Celsius scale places ordinary water's freezing point near zero degrees. Pressure and dissolved substances affect exact physical conditions.
answerNotes.FAHRENHEIT: Fahrenheit is widely used in United States forecasts. It places water's freezing point at 32 degrees under standard reference conditions.
answerNotes.MERCURY: Mercury was used in many traditional thermometers. Modern instruments may use other liquids or electronic sensors instead.
answerNotes.ALCOHOL: Alcohol-based liquids can make a visible expanding column. The particular liquid and coloring depend on the instrument.

title: A Compass in the Hand
description: Explore directions and the parts of a magnetic compass through plain descriptions of how its pointer and dial are read.
cardDescription: Explore directions and the parts of a magnetic compass through plain descriptions of how its pointer and dial are read.
focus: A magnetic compass responds to Earth’s magnetic field. Magnetic north and geographic north are different references, so the clues do not treat the instrument as automatically pointing to the exact geographic pole.
solvingTip: Separate the whole instrument from its pointer and direction markings. A bearing is a direction measurement rather than a place.
words: Magnetic instrument used to indicate directions
Magnetized pointer that turns inside a traditional direction-finding instrument
Direction expressed as an angle from a reference direction
Compass ___, diagram showing directions on a map or dial
Object producing a magnetic field, such as a compass needle
Direction opposite south on a standard compass card
Direction opposite north on a standard compass card
Direction opposite west on a standard compass card
Direction opposite east on a standard compass card
Marked circular face surrounding a direction pointer
Indicator showing a reading on an instrument
Protective outer housing of a pocket compass
To rotate an instrument or its movable ring
Drawing of an area used alongside direction information

answerNotes.COMPASS: A magnetic compass aligns with the local magnetic field. Its north reference differs from geographic true north by magnetic declination.
answerNotes.NEEDLE: The needle can rotate to align with the magnetic field. The surrounding case and markings do not perform that alignment.
answerNotes.BEARING: A bearing describes direction. It is different from a distance along a route.
answerNotes.ROSE: A compass rose displays directional references. The word rose names a diagram here rather than a flower.
answerNotes.MAGNET: A magnet interacts with other magnetic fields. This property allows a suitably supported needle to align with Earth's field.

title: Rain in a Garden Measuring Jar
description: Watch rain collect in a clear jar through water levels, marked lines, and a simple amount reading.
cardDescription: Watch rain collect in a clear jar through water levels, marked lines, and a simple amount reading.
subtheme: Rain in a Garden Measuring Jar
focus: The marks help compare collected amounts. These clues stay with familiar containers and weather words.
solvingTip: Start with a short container, weather, or pouring word.
words: Clear container collecting the rain in this scene
Water falling from clouds into the garden container
U.S. length unit used in many rainfall reports
Mark showing a level on the measuring container

Containing as much as the jar is meant to hold

Narrow hollow shape used in some rain collectors
Clear material forming this garden container

answerNotes.JAR: A marked container can make the collected amount easier to compare.
answerNotes.RAIN: Rain is liquid precipitation rather than falling ice or snow.
answerNotes.INCH: Rainfall depth is commonly reported in inches in the United States.
answerNotes.LINE: The water level is compared with the marked lines.
answerNotes.LEVEL: Level identifies the surface height rather than the weather forecast.

title: Light and Shadows
description: Look at the words for blocked, scattered, and reflected light through familiar objects such as mirrors and glass.
cardDescription: Look at the words for blocked, scattered, and reflected light through familiar objects such as mirrors and glass.
focus: Materials interact with light in different ways. A translucent material passes scattered light, an opaque one blocks direct transmission, and a mirror reflects light to form an image.
solvingTip: Choose the behavior described by the clue. Passing, blocking, bending, and reflecting light are different actions.
words: Not allowing visible light to pass through
Passing light while scattering it so details are blurred
To send light back from a surface
Transparent optical shape that can separate white light into colors
Darker region formed where an object blocks light from a source
Object or place from which light is emitted
Reflective surface used to form an image
Directed bundle of light traveling from a source
Measure of the turn between two light paths
Transparent solid used in many windows and lenses
Visible electromagnetic radiation reaching the eye
Having little or no visible illumination
Line used to represent a direction of light travel
Visual quality associated with different visible wavelengths

answerNotes.OPAQUE: Opaque describes blocked transmission. It does not mean a surface cannot reflect light.
answerNotes.TRANSLUCENT: Translucent differs from transparent, which allows a clearer view through a material. Both differ from opaque.
answerNotes.REFLECT: Reflection sends light back. Refraction changes its direction as it passes between materials.
answerNotes.PRISM: A prism can separate colors because different wavelengths refract by different amounts. It does not create those colors from nothing.
answerNotes.SHADOW: A shadow depends on the source, object, and receiving area. Its softness and size change with their geometry.

title: Magnets on the Fridge
description: Explore magnetic poles, familiar materials, and the words for forces acting across a small gap.
cardDescription: Explore magnetic poles, familiar materials, and the words for forces acting across a small gap.
focus: Not every metal is strongly attracted to an ordinary magnet. These clues focus on familiar magnetic behavior while separating the material, the field, and the direction of the force.
solvingTip: Use the relationship in the clue. Like and unlike poles behave differently, and a material name differs from the force acting on it.
words: Object producing a field that can attract iron
To push away magnetically, as two like poles do
To pull toward, as unlike magnetic poles do
Iron-based material commonly attracted to a refrigerator magnet
Region described by the magnetic influence around an object
Either end region of a bar magnet's strongest attraction
One of the two conventional magnetic pole names
Magnetic pole name paired with north
Metal strongly attracted by an ordinary magnet
Push or pull exerted in a magnetic interaction
Direction-finding instrument containing a freely turning magnet
Straight rectangular shape of a familiar classroom magnet
Closed curved path, as in a coil of wire
Material category that includes iron, copper, and aluminum

answerNotes.MAGNET: A magnet can attract certain materials strongly. It does not attract every metal in the same way.
answerNotes.REPEL: Like magnetic poles repel. Unlike poles attract, so the relationship between the poles matters.
answerNotes.ATTRACT: Attraction draws objects together. It is different from repulsion, which pushes them apart.
answerNotes.STEEL: Many steels are strongly magnetic, but some stainless steel types respond weakly or not at all. Steel is not a promise of identical magnetic behavior.
answerNotes.FIELD: A magnetic field can act across a gap. Its strength and direction vary with position.
